newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Meister urges honest meeting of EMU targets.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Meister urges honest meeting of EMU targets.

text.p: Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said on Tuesday it was important that European Union states meet the terms of membership of European currency union both honestly and punctually.

Speaking at a banking seminar in Mainz, Meister went on to lament the dollar's current "inappropriate" level against the mark. The dollar was at 1.49 marks on Tuesday evening, far below the heady levels of 1.54 marks attained in October.
"The current dollar exchange rate is not appropriate," Meister said when asked if the dollar's current standing was consistent with the fundamental economic situation in the U.S.

Meister said Germany must strive to meet the EMU starting deadline in 1999 and the chances of that happening were good. "We have to make the effort to meet the January 1, 1999 starting deadline for European currency union," he said.

In contrast to the dollar, Meister said current interest rates were appropriate. "The Bundesbank will continue to follow its current course. Interest rate levels are appropriate. There is no need for the Bundesbank to intervene," said Meister.

Meister warned nations against being tempted to use creative accounting methods or one-off windfalls to whip their finances into shape to enter Europe's currency union, echoing similar calls by other German policy makers on EMU criteria.

"Already when a nation's progress in meeting entry criteria to the currency union is reviewed, the acceptance of creative accounting and one-off measures must be ruled out," Meister said, adding that interest income should not be used to fill budget gaps.

He reasserted the Bundesbank's belief that currency union also had to be a stable union and said he backed the introduction of a stability pact which would trigger sanctions against nations deviating from fiscal austerity.
"An unsatisfactory quasi-automatic triggering of sanctions would lead to lax budget discipline," said Meister.
In addition, Meister underscored the difference in progress reports issued by the European Monetary Institute (EMI) and the European Union.
While the EMI -- the forerunner of the European Central Bank -- is distinctly more critical of nations' progress, the EU takes a slightly more relaxed attitude, Meister said.
He noted that the EU commission had no qualms about predicting that 12 of the total 15 European Union member nations will qualify for the currency union at the start.

"The group deliberately leaves open how lasting nations' efforts to meet convergence criteria will be," he said. He also said it was questionable whether a high measure of fiscal discipline was sustainable in the long-term.
Earlier in the day, his fellow Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said he believed a firmer dollar might seem more appropriate.
"A firmer U.S. dollar might seem more appropriate," Krupp the head of the regional state central bank of Hamburg, Mecklenburg and Schleswig-Holstein, said in an interview with a news agency.

Krupp said in the interview that the Bundesbank would consider cutting German interest rates again if the economy were to falter but said it would have no reason to cut rates if current projections for 1996 economic growth were confirmed.
Krupp said that there was no reason to change rates at the moment since inflation was not a concern and long-term interest rates were satisfactory.
